newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan parliament opens amid economic policy woes.
newsitem.headline: Japan parliament opens amid economic policy woes.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's economic policies look set to come under heavy fire in a session of parliament which opens on Monday, but opposition disarray could help dampen any threat to his administration.

The Tokyo stock market, racked by doubts about Hashimoto's commitment to reform and upset with his tight budget for the next business year, has already signalled its displeasure by a drastic fall which dragged the key 225-share Nikkei average to within a hair's breadth of 17,000 in early January.
The market sagged again on Monday morning ahead of Hashimoto's policy speech, undermined in part by fading hopes that the government would unveil steps to bolster share prices.
The key 225-share Nikkei average slid 466.36 points, or 2.58 percent, to 17,623.68 by midday and brokers said potential buyers remained cautious ahead of parliament's opening.
"Not only voters, but financial markets are keenly interested in the session of parliament which opens on January 20," said an editorial in financial daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun.
"Many people are looking for clues as to whether or not the structural reform of Japan on the brink of the 21st century will proceed from the debate in parliament," the paper said.

The stock market's decline has boosted pressure on Hashimoto to rethink his budget, implement real reforms and ease the fears about the economy that are battering share prices -- although the government has repeatedly said the outlook is not as grim as the market thinks.

Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita lent some support to that view on Monday, telling a central bank branch managers' meeting that Japan's economy was still gradually recovering and that the strength of that recovery was growing gradually.
Much of the recent market pessimism was sparked by Hashimoto's proposed tight budget for the 1997/98 fiscal year starting on April 1, which aims at getting Japan's big budget deficit under control.

Concern has focused not only on fears that a rise in the sales tax and an end to special income tax cuts could stall the economic recovery in its tracks, but on the apparent lack of commitment to reform signalled by a failure to reject pleas to fund special interests' pet projects.
A survey by Nihon Keizai Shimbun last week showed that while voter support for Hashimoto was a robust 47.1 percent, 86 percent were dissatisfied with his economic policies.

Political analysts said Hashimoto's first big test would be whether his government could pass its supplementary budget for 1996/97 by its self-imposed January 31 deadline and succeed in passing -- without revisions -- the budget for 1997/98 by the end of February. That would allow the 1997/98 budget to take effect even without Upper House approval.

But while Hashimoto may face some pressure from his two tiny partners to make changes in the 2.67 trillion yen ($22.8 billion) extra budget, opposition parties look too weak to succeed in forcing major reforms to the 1997/98 budget, analysts said.
"I don't see the opposition getting together and cooperating. They're too weak and divided," said Jeff Young, political analyst at Salomon Brothers Asia.

That means Hashimoto could ride out the rough time in parliament, barring a serious slump that takes the Nikkei to around 15,000 -- the crisis level which erases banks' hidden profits on shareholdings and pushes many into the red.
"His idea is to stiffen his resolve and rely on his near-majority and opposition weakness to stick it out," Young said. ($1=117 yen)
